t: Two Out of Three - Presence Counting with Sets and Bitmasks
o: From three arrays we must return the distinct values that occur in at least two different arrays; repetitions inside one array are irrelevant. In example 2, values 1, 2 and 3 each appear in two arrays, so all three are returned; in example 3 nothing overlaps and the answer is empty. Sizes and values are capped at 100, so any reasonable bookkeeping passes - the interesting choice is between presence counters and bitmasks.
k: Only presence matters, not frequency - deduplicate each array before counting.
A value qualifies based on how many distinct arrays contain it, so count arrays, not occurrences.
Values are bounded by 100, so a fixed bitmask per value replaces hashing entirely.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash Sets and Presence Counts
a.i: Insert the distinct values of each array into a shared map from value to the number of arrays containing it. Every value whose counter reaches at least two belongs to the answer.
s: For each of the three arrays, collect its distinct values.
Increment a counter for every distinct value found.
Collect values whose counter is at least two.
a.t: O(n1 + n2 + n3) - constant work per element plus a pass over distinct values.
a.sp: O(U) - at most U distinct values stored, U bounded by the union of the arrays.

a.i: Assign bit b to array b and OR it into mask[value] whenever that value occurs in array b. Afterwards, a value belongs to the answer exactly when its mask has at least two bits set. Fixed-size indexing means no hashing, deterministic memory, and a natural extension to more arrays.
s: For each array b and each element x, set mask[x] |= 1 << b.
Scan v from 1 to 100 and output every v with popcount(mask[v]) >= 2.
a.t: O(n1 + n2 + n3 + V) with V = 100 candidate values scanned at the end.

w: Say "presence, not frequency" immediately - it is the entire trick, since a value duplicated within one array must not qualify on its own. Remember the answer may be empty and its order is irrelevant. The bitmask view generalizes gracefully: k arrays fit in one machine word up to k = 32, and switching the predicate to popcount == 2 answers "exactly two arrays". Expect that generalization as the follow-up.
